input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed is placed in contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the component that permeates through the membrane as a vapour. In this work, flux is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), and the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed. A polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane were both tested using a feed consisting of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at a temperature of 60 °C. The polymer membrane was found to give a flux of 1.6 kg m-2 h-1 together with a separation factor of 180, although its flux fell by 7% over the course of 500 h. The zeolite membrane, by contrast, gave a flux of 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 320, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h, within the limits of measurement error. It can therefore be seen that the zeolite membrane is the more selective of the two membranes, whilst the polymer membrane is the more permeable, and the stability results separate them still further, since the zeolite membrane maintained its flux throughout the duration of the test whereas the polymer membrane did not. It should be noted that this comparison is based on a single feed composition, and that no test was run beyond 500 h; flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for one and the same membrane, and the comparison that has been presented here applies to the feed and the duration that were actually tested.

Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), and the separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed. A polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane were tested on a feed of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C. The polymer membrane gave a flux of 1.6 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 180, and its flux fell 7% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 320, and its flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The zeolite membrane is the more selective of the two and the polymer membrane the more permeable, and the stability record separates them further: the zeolite held its flux over the test duration and the polymer did not. The ranking rests on one feed composition, as tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h; flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the comparison is stated for the tested feed, at the tested temperature, and for the tested duration alone.
